claims.text: Atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity in high-entropy alloys creates a wide distribution of local stacking-fault energies.
The distribution of local stacking-fault energies promotes coordinated activation of deformation twinning and dislocation slip.
Coordinated twinning and dislocation slip promote deformation delocalization and delay necking failure.
This mechanism produces a superior strength–ductility combination under dynamic loading.
CoCrFeNi or CoCrFeNi-based nanopillars possess atomic compositional heterogeneities that generate spatial variations in stacking-fault energy.
Extended homogenization heat treatment will reduce the relevant atomic-scale compositional fluctuations relative to the as-cast or minimally homogenized state.
Both dislocation slip and deformation twinning are active during room-temperature tensile deformation of CoCrFeNi nanopillars.
The proposed mechanism applies at moderate dynamic strain rates.
The proposed mechanism applies from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures.
Interfaces between regions predisposed to twinning and regions predisposed to slip mediate strain delocalization.
Chemical heterogeneity generates a broad distribution of energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Regions with lower local stacking-fault energy activate deformation twinning early.
Regions adjacent to the twinning-prone regions accommodate strain through dislocation slip.
An as-cast or minimally homogenized HEA will have greater tensile strength and uniform elongation than a homogenized sample under otherwise identical dynamic loading.
The more chemically heterogeneous sample will exhibit extensive deformation twinning and dislocation activity.
Samples processed to minimize compositional heterogeneity will show less twin formation and weaker strength–ductility synergy.
The hypothesis should hold broadly for FCC high-entropy alloys under dynamic deformation.
The mechanism may cease to apply when composition changes induce phase transformations or precipitation-dominated deformation.
Dynamic recrystallization or evolution of local chemical order may also influence the mechanical response in different high-entropy alloys.
